It is Wednesday, August 5th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national picture this morning still feels like a collision between public risk, legal risk and political risk. Those pressures may look separate on the surface, but they all feed into confidence, spending, policy and the broader cost of capital.

The first story is still Spokane, and it remains the clearest continuity story from the start of the week. The Associated Press reported on August 4 that authorities arrested a Spokane man on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire, the largest of the blazes that have ripped through the area. AP reported that the fires have destroyed at least 700 buildings and forced tens of thousands of people from their homes. The reason this stays in the lead is that it is no longer only a weather and firefighting story. It is now also a housing-loss story, an insurance story, a municipal recovery story and potentially a criminal accountability story, which means it is moving deeper into the territory that affects rebuilding timelines and public resources.

The second story is the latest state challenge to the administration’s trade policy. AP reported on August 4 that 25 states sued the Trump administration over its new tariffs, arguing the White House is using the measures as a substitute for tariffs that the Supreme Court had already struck down earlier this year. The latest tariffs reportedly range from 10 percent to 12.5 percent and hit countries that account for nearly all American imports. That matters because when tariff policy moves from policy announcement to immediate multistate litigation, businesses have to price not just the cost increase but also the uncertainty around how durable the policy really is. For lenders, borrowers and developers, that kind of uncertainty works its way into materials costs, underwriting assumptions and inflation expectations.

The third story is another clash between states and Washington, but this one cuts closer to household behavior. AP reported on August 4 that more than 20 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the federal government from gaining wide access to the personal information of Temporary Assistance for Needy Families recipients. According to AP, the states argue the new rule would allow immigration status, Social Security numbers and other personal information to be shared more broadly across government. Even if this stays framed as a legal and privacy fight, the economic read-through is that households respond when they think core support systems may carry new risks. That can change willingness to seek help, and changes in that behavior ripple through local economies.

The fourth story is the political temperature check from Tuesday’s primaries. AP’s election takeaways on August 4 said the Michigan Senate primary exposed a visible divide inside the Democratic Party between establishment and progressive wings, while Republicans in Michigan also tested the continued power of President Trump’s endorsement in the governor’s race. AP also pointed to nomination outcomes in Missouri and Virginia that will shape the fall map. This matters because political messaging is still converging around affordability, executive power, immigration and institutional trust. Those are not abstract campaign themes anymore. They are the same themes businesses and markets are already trying to handicap.

So the national frame this morning is fairly direct. Spokane remains a live recovery and accountability story. States are escalating legal fights over tariffs and benefits data. And the primary results underscore that both parties are still being pulled by the same affordability and trust questions dominating the broader economy. With that set, let’s turn to debt.

Debt Desk

In rates and financing, the cleanest way to read this morning is that the market is open, but it is still selective, and the long end is still the part of the curve doing the most work in every underwriting conversation.

Using the project’s market-data checker against the official Treasury table for August 4, the latest completed Treasury closes are 4.20 percent on the 2-year, 4.33 percent on the 5-year, 4.63 percent on the 10-year and 5.18 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for August 3. That is a slightly friendlier setup than the uglier moments we saw late last week, but it is not easy money. The front end is still restrictive, the belly of the curve is still carrying real cost, and the 30-year is still high enough to keep many permanent-debt decisions uncomfortable.

That term-structure point matters. A 2-year Treasury around 4.20 and a 5-year around 4.33 still keep short-duration and floating executions from feeling cheap once lender spread, cap cost and reserve requirements are added back in. A 10-year around 4.63 is better than the market’s more anxious prints from recent sessions, but a 30-year above 5.10 still tells you duration is expensive and investors want to be paid for it. For borrowers, that means the shape of the curve still argues for discipline on leverage, structure and business-plan timing, not optimism for its own sake.

The big official policy backdrop remains Treasury supply. On August 3, Treasury said it now expects July-through-September net marketable borrowing of $739 billion. Even before today’s refunding discussion fully hits the market, that estimate is enough to keep duration supply in the conversation. More borrowing does not automatically blow out loan coupons, but it does reinforce the idea that long-dated yields may stay sticky unless buyers are convinced inflation and growth are both cooling enough to justify lower term premiums.

Fresh market-color research from CBRE, released August 3, points to a market that is still functioning even with those rate headwinds. CBRE said its Lending Momentum Index remained historically elevated in the second quarter, with the number of commercial loans up 11 percent year over year and average loan size up 5 percent, while spreads and loan-to-value ratios tightened. The useful read-through there is that lenders are competing more on price than on leverage. That is a constructive sign, but it is not a loose sign. Borrowers are still earning proceeds with cleaner assets, better sponsorship and clearer exit visibility.

The lender mix behind that tone is important. CBRE said alternative lenders and banks led non-agency deals in the quarter, and MBA’s recap of the report said multifamily loan spreads tightened by 15 basis points year over year to 162 basis points while debt-fund activity continued to grow. Put that together with current market quotes from Northmarq dated August 4 and you get a practical execution map for this morning. Life company multifamily money is still generally landing around spreads of roughly 115 to 170 basis points over Treasuries for stronger permanent loans, while CMBS is still materially wider, generally around 175 to 225 over on 10-year structures and 210 to 250 over on 5-year structures. That spread gap is one reason life company money still looks attractive for low-leverage institutional deals, while CMBS remains more situational and debt funds keep their edge on heavier lifts, mezz pieces and transitional business plans.

You can see that selective-but-open backdrop in the deal flow from August 4. Walker & Dunlop arranged a $137.5 million refinancing for 12 Halsey, a newly completed Class A mixed-use multifamily property in Brooklyn. That is a useful signal for sponsors with high-quality urban multifamily because it shows large permanent or near-permanent executions are still available when completion risk has largely burned off. On the construction side, Concord Summit Capital announced a $50 million construction loan for the 268-unit Vic Centre Apartments project in Fort Worth, structured with senior debt plus mezzanine financing at 80 percent loan-to-cost. Capital City Real Estate also announced the closing of construction financing for the 318-unit Spivey Grove development in metro Atlanta, with Protective Life providing the construction loan. Those three items together say the market is still funding multifamily, but often with stacked capital, tighter structure and a clear preference for sponsors who can explain the exit.

Agency execution also remains a major stabilizer. Greystone announced on August 3 that it provided $105.8 million in Freddie Mac refinancing for two multifamily communities in El Cajon, California. That follows the August 3 confirmation that Zions completed its acquisition of Basis Multifamily Finance’s agency lending platform, expanding its Fannie Mae DUS and Freddie Mac Optigo footprint. The message is straightforward: agency channels remain one of the most reliable ways to keep apartment liquidity moving, and lenders still want more capacity there because the conventional market has not become easy enough to make agency relevance fade.

FHA remains part of that same story. Northmarq’s August 4 rate sheet shows 223(f) refinancing generally in a range of roughly 5.75 to 6.20 percent before mortgage insurance premium, with 221(d)(4) construction-perm executions broadly around 6.20 to 6.65 percent before MIP. In a market where conventional fixed-rate debt can still feel punitive for borrowers who need duration and leverage, that FHA lane keeps mattering, especially for preservation, affordable execution and deals that can tolerate process in exchange for structure.

On the risk side, the securitized market is still warning against complacency. Trepp wrote on August 4 that the August 2026 private-label CMBS hard-maturity cohort totals $5.49 billion across 130 loan pieces, roughly double July’s volume, and said refinancing is likely to be challenging for the $3.04 billion carrying a current debt yield below 8 percent. That is not a multifamily-only story, but it matters for the whole market because maturity pressure keeps feeding back into valuations, recap decisions and lender behavior. Trepp also published fresh work on August 4 showing meaningful divergence across community banks with multifamily concentrations, with the broad read-through that supply-supportive government programs are helping but income-based restrictions and legacy credit stress are still biting. In plain English, better multifamily assets are financeable, but the sector is not uniformly healthy.

That is why execution tone still needs to be described lender by lender. Banks are in the market for cleaner multifamily, industrial and relationship-driven credits, but they still look measured on leverage and construction exposure. Life companies remain disciplined and want sponsorship, quality and debt-service coverage they can defend. CMBS is available, but borrowers are still paying for it and the market is not pretending that refinance risk has disappeared. Debt funds remain essential for stretch senior, mezzanine and transitional assignments because they can move faster and solve around complexity, but that flexibility still comes with a cost. Agency lenders remain the cleanest repeatable outlet for many apartment borrowers, and FHA remains the duration answer when process is manageable and proceeds matter.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury closes for August 4 are 4.20 percent on the 2-year, 4.33 percent on the 5-year, 4.63 percent on the 10-year and 5.18 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for August 3. Treasury’s current-quarter borrowing estimate is $739 billion. CRE lending volume and average loan size improved in the second quarter, but execution is still tiered by asset quality and lender type. Multifamily financing is active across agency, life company, bank and structured-construction channels, yet CMBS maturities and multifamily credit divergence still argue for caution.

One thing to watch today is whether the long end can stay orderly as Treasury supply remains front and center. If the 10-year can hold in the mid-4s and the 30-year stays closer to 5.15 than 5.30, more borrowers may decide this is good enough to move on refinancing and takeout conversations. If long duration backs up again, expect more deals to lean on mezzanine, preferred equity, bridge extensions and staggered capital stacks instead of a clean one-shot permanent solution.

The Wednesday takeaway is that the national mood is still being shaped by disaster response, legal escalation and political sorting, while the debt market is still being shaped by term-premium pressure, selective lender competition and a strong divide between financeable stories and stressed stories. Capital is there. It is just still asking harder questions before it commits.

AP’s election coverage says voters in Michigan, Missouri and Virginia are heading into closely watched primaries that could shape the Senate map, several House races and the broader direction of both parties going into the midterms. That matters because the political center of gravity is still unsettled. Candidates are being forced to speak more directly about affordability, immigration, public safety and executive power, which means the next round of political messaging is likely to keep colliding with the same economic concerns markets are already pricing.

So the national picture this morning is fairly direct. The wildfire story around Spokane has worsened and now includes an arson arrest. States are pressing fresh legal challenges over tariffs and over federal access to welfare-recipient data. Congress is trying to buy time with another stopgap spending plan. And primary voters are testing both parties on the issues that have been driving national friction all summer. With that backdrop in place, let’s turn to debt.

Debt Desk

Now to the rates and execution picture, and today the right way to read it is to separate what is officially fixed from what is still moving in real time.

As of this early Tuesday run, the latest completed Treasury closes are from Monday, August 3. Market data compiled by Investing.com show the 2-year closed at 4.256 percent, the 5-year at 4.398 percent, the 10-year at 4.684 percent and the 30-year at 5.229 percent. The latest official SOFR print from the New York Fed is 3.66 percent for Friday, July 31. Put that together and the shape of the market is still the same one we have been talking about: the front end is restrictive, the belly is not cheap, and the long bond is still expensive enough to keep permanent debt decisions uncomfortable.

That matters because Monday’s rally in stocks and pullback in yields did not suddenly make financing easy. It just took the edge off the panic that hit the long end late last week. A 2-year in the mid-4s and a 5-year just under 4.40 still mean floating-rate and shorter-reset executions carry real carry cost once lender spread, cap economics and reserves are layered in. A 10-year around 4.68 and a 30-year above 5.20 still leave many sponsors staring at fixed-rate proceeds and asking whether the certainty is worth the payment shock.

One fresh policy headline in the debt world came straight from Treasury. On Monday, August 3, the Treasury Department raised its July-through-September net marketable borrowing estimate to $739 billion, up $68 billion from the prior estimate. That does not instantly change a single loan quote, but it does reinforce the supply conversation hanging over the long end. When investors are already debating whether term yields deserve to stay high, a larger borrowing need gives the market one more reason to keep demanding compensation for duration.

You can also see the market’s current execution map in the fresh deal tape. Walker & Dunlop said on August 3 that it arranged a $137.5 million refinancing for 12 Halsey, a newly completed Class A mixed-use multifamily property in Brooklyn. That is a useful signal because it shows capital still showing up for high-quality urban multifamily once lease-up and completion risk are largely behind the deal. In other words, stabilized or nearly stabilized apartment product can still clear at real size, but the market wants maturity in the business plan before it gets comfortable.

Another important fresh multifamily item came from Zions Bancorporation on August 3. Zions said it completed its acquisition of the agency lending platform of Basis Multifamily Finance, including the team, capabilities and servicing rights tied to that business. The bank said the move expands its participation in Fannie Mae’s DUS program and Freddie Mac’s Optigo conventional program. That may sound like a corporate strategy footnote, but it is worth attention because it points to a bigger theme: lenders still want scalable multifamily channels, especially where agency execution can deliver repeat volume with established credit structures.

The broader tone across lender types still looks mixed but functional. Banks appear more willing than they were a year ago to compete for cleaner multifamily and industrial loans, especially where sponsorship is strong and deposits or broader relationships matter. Life companies remain selective and disciplined, but they are in the conversation for lower-leverage permanent multifamily if the asset is institutional and the sponsor can tolerate conservative proceeds. CMBS is open when scale and structure line up, though it is still not behaving like effortless takeout liquidity. Debt funds continue to do a large share of the heavier lifting on transitional multifamily, completion risk, recapitalizations and any situation where speed and creativity matter more than raw coupon.

That last point is one reason securitized surveillance still matters so much. Trepp’s July 2026 CMBS delinquency report, published on July 31, showed the overall CMBS delinquency rate jumping 51 basis points to 7.86 percent. More importantly for this audience, Trepp said multifamily posted the largest property-type increase, rising 46 basis points to 7.69 percent as a wave of apartment loans in Ohio, Texas and New York turned 30 days delinquent. That is the key reminder not to get lazy with the multifamily story. Apartments are still one of the most financeable sectors in commercial real estate, but legacy floating-rate paper and maturity stress are still producing damage beneath the surface.

The agency lane is still doing a lot of the stabilization work. Freddie Mac’s second-quarter 2026 results, released July 30, said multifamily new business activity reached $18 billion in the quarter, with 66 percent of year-to-date activity supporting mission-driven affordable housing. Fannie Mae’s second-quarter results, released July 29, said multifamily acquisition volume reached $14.2 billion in the quarter and the multifamily serious delinquency rate improved to 0.60 percent from 0.78 percent. Those are not brand-new headlines today, but they remain the latest official agency scorecard, and the message is that agency liquidity is still present, especially where affordability and stabilized cash flow are part of the story.

HUD and FHA remain relevant for the same reason. The latest official SOFR print may sit at 3.66 percent, but that does not make conventional permanent debt broadly comfortable. For borrowers that can live with the process, HUD-backed execution still offers a meaningful path to duration and structure in a market where conventional fixed-rate debt often feels punitive. That is why the FHA lane continues to matter even when the headline flow is quieter than the debt-fund tape.

The consumer mortgage backdrop is also still reinforcing multifamily demand. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey showed the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.66 percent as of July 30, up from 6.58 percent the prior week. High mortgage rates do not solve apartment financing problems, but they do keep the buy-versus-rent equation supportive for many households, which in turn helps underpin occupancy and rent collections in better-positioned multifamily product.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. Monday’s Treasury closes put the 2-year at 4.256 percent, the 5-year at 4.398 percent, the 10-year at 4.684 percent and the 30-year at 5.229 percent. The latest official SOFR print is 3.66 percent for July 31. Treasury has increased its current-quarter borrowing estimate, keeping duration supply in focus. Fresh multifamily execution is still happening, as shown by the Brooklyn refinancing and by Zions expanding its agency lending footprint. But CMBS surveillance still says apartment stress has not cleared, especially in older floating-rate and maturity-challenged paper.

One thing to watch today is whether the market treats Monday’s yield pullback as a real reset or just a pause after last week’s selloff. If the 10-year stays under about 4.70 and the 30-year holds closer to 5.20 than 5.30, some borrowers may decide the window is good enough to move on permanent debt or agency takeouts. If the long end backs up again on supply concerns, inflation anxiety or another geopolitical swing, expect more borrowers to keep leaning on bridge debt, structured equity and staggered capital stacks rather than locking expensive fixed-rate money all at once.

The Tuesday takeaway is that the market is still open, but it remains highly conditional. Nationally, the country is balancing disaster response, legal conflict and election pressure. In Debt Desk, yields have eased from last week’s extremes but remain restrictive, Treasury supply is still part of the long-end conversation, fresh multifamily deals are getting done for the right assets, agencies are still providing ballast, and CMBS data are still warning that not every apartment story is healthy just because the sector remains the market favorite. Credit is available. It is simply making borrowers prove more before it says yes.

item.description: Spokane wildfire evacuations, Idaho shooting developments, cyberattacks on Midwestern water systems, and the latest political and rate-pressure backdrop lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to the verified Treasury curve, SOFR, multifamily financing activity, CMBS stress, agency production, HUD-backed execution, lender tone, a concise markets snapshot, and one thing to watch for August 3, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday, August 3rd, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national picture coming into this Monday feels unsettled in exactly the way credit markets notice. The stories at the top of the tape are about disruption, security, public confidence and cost pressure, and together they give you a pretty clean read on the mood that borrowers, lenders and investors are bringing into the week.

The first story this morning is the wildfire emergency in eastern Washington. The Associated Press reported Monday, August 3, that fires near Spokane had already destroyed about 600 homes, businesses and other structures and forced roughly 60,000 people to evacuate. AP said the fires remained uncontained Sunday, and officials were warning there may not be much weather relief in the next couple of days. We have been tracking the broader heat-and-fire story since the weekend, but this is a meaningful escalation. Once the conversation moves from elevated risk to actual large-scale evacuations, destroyed structures and pressure on hospitals and local infrastructure, it stops being only a weather headline. It becomes a housing, insurance and municipal capacity story as well, and that matters nationally.

The second story is the new detail out of Twin Falls, Idaho, after the mass shooting at a newly opened In-N-Out. AP reported Sunday, August 2, that police now say the gunman, identified as 24-year-old Chad Williams, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound and acted alone. Authorities said four people are dead including the shooter, seven others were injured, and two of those victims remained in critical condition as of Sunday. That update matters because it shifts the story from the immediate shock of the attack into the next phase, which is motive, security and community response. These incidents very quickly become confidence events for local employers, retailers and families, and the unresolved questions tend to hang over a place long after the crime scene clears.

The third story is infrastructure security, and it is getting more attention for good reason. AP reported Sunday, August 2, that Michigan joined Minnesota in reporting cyberattacks on water systems, though state officials said the affected systems were still operating safely. On its face that might sound narrow, but it really is not. Water systems are basic critical infrastructure, and when multiple states are reporting cyber incidents in the same window, it becomes a resilience story with national implications. It also reinforces the broader point that local public systems are now carrying a bigger operational-security burden even when nothing dramatic is visible to the public at street level.

The fourth story is political, but it ties back to policy credibility and market confidence. AP reported Monday, August 3, that Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche formally terminated the $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund that had been designed to compensate Trump political allies, after Republican senators threatened to block his nomination for attorney general. The reason this lands in a national brief is not the personalities. It is the signal that intra-party bargaining is still shaping governance in visible ways even on headline matters that were previously framed as settled. Washington process risk is not the only thing markets care about, but it still affects how investors think about policy follow-through.

The fifth story is the economic backdrop hanging over all of this. AP reported Monday, August 3, on a new AP-NORC poll showing immigration remains a political strength for President Trump within the Republican base even as approval on the economy has weakened, with only 32 percent of U.S. adults approving of his handling of the economy. That lines up with the broader affordability theme we have been following. People do not experience the economy through abstract gross domestic product tables. They experience it through rent, insurance, prescription costs, grocery bills and debt service. When confidence on the economy softens while financing costs stay elevated, that matters for spending behavior and for political risk heading deeper into the second half of the year.

So the national setup this morning is pretty clear. The West is dealing with a fast-moving wildfire disaster around Spokane, Idaho is still absorbing the aftermath of a deadly public shooting, Midwestern water systems are dealing with cyber incidents, Washington is still showing policy friction, and voters remain uneasy about the economy. With that as the backdrop, let’s turn to debt.

Debt Desk

Now to the rates and execution picture, and as always we are going to anchor this to the latest official prints available at run time.

The latest official Treasury curve available this morning is the Friday, July 31 close from the U.S. Treasury. That is 4.28 percent on the 2-year, 4.45 percent on the 5-year, 4.75 percent on the 10-year and 5.27 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for July 30. Those are still the numbers that matter coming into Monday because they tell you the market is not just pricing higher-for-longer at the front end. It is also still charging a lot for duration.

That is the first thing borrowers need to keep in mind this week. A 2-year at 4.28 percent and a 5-year at 4.45 percent already keep short and intermediate debt expensive once you layer in lender spread, reserves and structure. But the bigger issue for permanent financing remains the back end of the curve. A 10-year at 4.75 percent and a 30-year at 5.27 percent make fixed-rate certainty feel expensive enough that plenty of sponsors are still asking whether it is better to lock now or buy time and hope for a friendlier takeout window later.

You can see that tradeoff very clearly in the financing tape. Commercial Observer reported on July 31 that Izo Capital provided a $25.6 million senior construction loan to help Sundance Properties finish phase one of the Flats at Alpine Junction in Alpine, Wyoming. That is exactly the kind of deal debt funds keep winning in this market: supply-constrained location, real housing demand, but a capital need that calls for speed, flexibility and comfort with completion risk. It is not the cheapest money on the board, but it is often the money that actually closes.

On the other side of the execution map, Commercial Observer also reported July 31 that Dwight Capital closed a HUD 223(f) refinancing of roughly $23.5 million for the 104-unit Station at Passaic Phase II in New Jersey. That tells you the government-backed lane is still very much open for the right stabilized apartment story. Borrowers that can live with the process and documentation burden are still finding HUD to be a durable solution when they want long-term structure instead of more bridge risk.

And then there is the blended-capital version of the market. Commercial Observer reported July 30 that Hudson Investing secured about $52.1 million of acquisition financing for Maple Knoll Apartments in Westfield, Indiana, with Torchlight Investors providing equity and Northmarq arranging the stack and providing senior debt through its Freddie Mac platform. That is an important signal because more deals are getting done with multiple capital providers solving different parts of the same problem. The market is functioning, but it is functioning through tailored stacks, not effortless single-source proceeds.

When you line those deals up, the execution tone is fairly consistent with what we have been tracking. Banks are still in the market, but mostly for cleaner sponsorship, stronger cash flow and relationships they already know well. Life companies remain competitive where leverage is modest and asset quality is high, especially in multifamily, but the long end of the Treasury curve keeps them disciplined on proceeds. CMBS is available when scale, sponsorship and loan structure line up, but it is not acting like automatic liquidity. Debt funds continue to do a disproportionate amount of the work on construction completion, recapitalizations, transitional multifamily and anything else that needs creativity or speed. That last point is partly inference from the deal mix, but the tape keeps supporting it.

The securitized market still deserves close attention, especially for apartments. KBRA reported on July 31 that the 30-plus-day delinquency rate in its private-label CMBS universe rose 29 basis points in July to 7.8 percent, while the distress rate climbed to 10.1 percent. KBRA also said the multifamily distress rate jumped 73 basis points in July after two straight monthly declines, with 23 multifamily loans newly becoming distressed. That is one of the clearest reminders available right now that multifamily is still the preferred story in commercial real estate, but it is not a clean story. Older floating-rate paper, maturity pressure and business plans underwritten to a friendlier rate regime are still working through the system.

The MBA data adds a second layer to that read. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported on July 30 that delinquency rates for commercial properties decreased in the second quarter across several lender groups, including banks, life companies and CMBS. CMBS delinquency came down to 4.82 percent from 5.21 percent, life company delinquencies fell to 1.19 percent from 1.23 percent, and bank delinquencies moved to 0.95 percent from 1.05 percent. That is constructive, but it does not mean committees are suddenly generous. The better interpretation is that system stress is being absorbed more steadily, even while new-loan underwriting remains selective.

On the agency side, the latest official second-quarter results still matter because they give you the cleanest current read on multifamily liquidity. Freddie Mac said on July 30 that multifamily new business activity reached $18 billion in the second quarter, up 58 percent from a year earlier, with 66 percent of year-to-date activity tied to mission-driven affordable housing. Fannie Mae said in second-quarter results released July 29 that multifamily delivered $14.2 billion in acquisition volume during the quarter, its guaranty book of business grew to about $544.6 billion, and its multifamily serious delinquency rate improved to 0.60 percent from 0.78 percent at the prior quarter end. Put simply, the agencies are still providing ballast, even if the day-to-day headline flow is quieter than the debt fund tape.

HUD and FHA remain part of that ballast too. Beyond the Dwight execution, HUD’s May 2026 FHA commercial mortgage portfolio report shows multifamily insurance in force ending the month at about $140.4 billion, with just two new 60-plus-day defaults added during May and total 60-plus-day defaults ending at 27 loans. That does not mean risk is absent, but it does reinforce the point that the FHA-insured multifamily book is operating from a different credit posture than the more stressed pockets of private-label multifamily finance.

The broader housing cost picture still matters for multifamily capital markets as well. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey shows the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.66 percent as of July 30, up from 6.58 percent the prior week. When mortgage rates stay this elevated, renter demand support does not disappear, and that continues to help apartment fundamentals at the margin even while financing remains tough.

There is also a broader capital-markets read-through here. We have been tracking the tension between political pressure for lower rates and a market that keeps refusing to hand out cheap long-term money. As long as that tension persists, commercial real estate borrowers should assume lender conversations will stay grounded in debt yield, refinance risk and downside protection, not in some near-term expectation that the market will bail out aggressive basis.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The official curve is 4.28 percent on the 2-year, 4.45 percent on the 5-year, 4.75 percent on the 10-year and 5.27 percent on the 30-year, and the latest official SOFR print is 3.65 percent for July 30. Fresh multifamily deals are still getting done through debt funds, HUD-backed refinancing and blended debt-plus-equity executions. CMBS remains open, but July surveillance data still show real stress, including in apartments. Agencies remain active, and high mortgage rates continue to support the rental demand argument even as they complicate the broader housing market.

One thing to watch this week is whether the long end of the Treasury curve can ease at all once the market fully digests the mix of slower growth, sticky affordability pressure and another heavy news cycle. If the 10-year stays around 4.75 percent and the 30-year stays above 5.25 percent, expect more borrowers to lean on bridge, agency or structured-capital solutions instead of rushing into conventional fixed-rate executions. If the back end softens even a little, some permanent-debt borrowers may decide this market is still not ideal, but finally close enough.

The Monday takeaway is that capital is available, but it is demanding precision. Nationally, the country is dealing with wildfire displacement, public-safety trauma, infrastructure security worries and softer economic confidence. In Debt Desk, the curve is still expensive, debt funds are still carrying a lot of the harder multifamily and transitional workload, agencies and HUD remain essential stabilizers, and CMBS surveillance is still flashing caution even as some delinquency data improve. The market is open. It just keeps asking harder questions before it says yes.

It is Sunday, August 2nd, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the morning brief, because the national picture heading into this Sunday still comes back to the same theme we have been tracking for borrowers and lenders alike. The country is dealing with a mix of physical disruption, household-cost pressure and an economic backdrop that is not breaking cleanly in either direction. Nothing feels fully resolved, and that is exactly the kind of environment where credit people start paying closer attention to execution risk.

The first story this morning is the dangerous weather and wildfire setup across the West. The Associated Press reported late Saturday, August 1, that a wind-driven fire near Spokane, Washington forced evacuations after the Old Trails Fire spread rapidly toward residential areas, jumped the Spokane River and burned through roughly four square miles with no containment by nightfall. AP also reported Saturday that the broader heat wave was pushing temperatures toward records across the West and sharply increasing fire danger from Washington to Oregon and beyond. That matters nationally because this is no longer just a local weather story. It is an infrastructure story, an insurance story and a municipal-capacity story all at once. When power shutoffs, evacuation orders and emergency declarations start stacking up, the cost is felt far beyond the immediate burn zone.

The second story is the deadly shooting in Twin Falls, Idaho. AP reported late Saturday, August 1, that three people were killed and seven others were injured in a shooting at a newly opened In-N-Out Burger, with authorities saying there was no ongoing threat by the evening but that key questions about the motive and exact sequence of events were still unresolved. In a national brief, the reason to stay with this story is not spectacle. It is the way these incidents instantly become confidence events for communities, employers and consumers. The facts are still developing, but the pattern is familiar: a crowded everyday retail location becomes a crime scene, families wait for answers and officials have to rebuild basic trust in public safety almost immediately.

The third story stays on household costs. AP reported on Friday, July 31, that the Trump administration is ending the temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that had helped keep prescription-drug plan premiums from jumping more sharply. The policy change does not hit every beneficiary the same way, but it lands in an economy where monthly bills still define how people judge conditions. For markets, this is one more sign that the affordability conversation is not cooling down. Even when inflation data stop accelerating, voters and consumers keep feeling pressure through rent, food, insurance, debt service and healthcare. That matters because cost fatigue has a way of shaping politics and spending behavior long before it shows up neatly in an economic release.

The fourth story is the macro backdrop behind all of that. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on Thursday, July 30, that real U.S. gross domestic product grew at a 1.5 percent annual rate in the second quarter, down from 2.1 percent in the first quarter. On the same release cycle, BEA showed the June personal consumption expenditures price index up 3.7 percent from a year earlier, with core PCE at 3.3 percent. That is not recession language, but it is also not the easy disinflation story many borrowers would prefer. Add in Freddie Mac’s Thursday reading that the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.66 percent, the highest level in a year, and the takeaway is straightforward. Growth is still there, but it is slower. Inflation is cooler than the worst levels, but it is still too warm. And financing costs remain high enough to keep pressure on both households and real estate.

So that is the national setup this Sunday morning. The West is dealing with a dangerous fire and heat pattern, Idaho is waking up to the aftermath of a mass shooting, healthcare affordability is back in the political conversation, and the economy still looks like it is expanding under a heavier rate burden than most borrowers want to carry. With that frame in place, let’s turn to debt.

Debt Desk

Now to the part of the morning where we anchor everything to the latest available official market prints instead of guessing from mood.

As of this run on Sunday, August 2, the latest official Treasury par yield curve available from the U.S. Treasury is the Friday, July 31 close. Treasury’s own data center shows the 2-year at 4.28 percent, the 5-year at 4.45 percent, the 10-year at 4.75 percent and the 30-year at 5.27 percent. The latest published SOFR print available from the New York Fed, via FRED, is 3.65 percent for Thursday, July 30.

That curve still tells a very specific story. The front end is not cheap, but it is not the whole problem. A 2-year at 4.28 and a 5-year at 4.45 mean short and intermediate money still costs real money, especially once credit spread and structure are layered in. But the real pressure continues to build as you move out the curve. A 10-year at 4.75 and a 30-year at 5.27 say duration remains expensive and certainty still carries a meaningful premium. In practical terms, that keeps permanent debt selective and keeps floating-rate or shorter-duration solutions alive for borrowers who think they can earn their way into a better takeout later.

You can see that in the financing tape from the last twenty-four to forty-eight hours. Commercial Observer reported on Friday, July 31, that Izo Capital provided $25.6 million of construction financing for Sundance Properties to bring a multifamily project in Alpine, Wyoming across the finish line. That is a useful signal because it looks like the kind of transaction debt funds are still built to win: a specific execution need, a project with enough conviction behind it, and a sponsor that needs flexibility more than it needs the lowest possible coupon.

A second financing signal came from New Jersey. Commercial Observer reported on Friday that Dwight Capital closed a HUD 223(f) refinancing for the 104-unit Station at Passaic Phase II. That is the other side of the market map. When the asset is stabilized enough and the borrower is willing to tolerate process in exchange for structure, the government-backed lane remains very relevant. In a high long-end rate environment, borrowers are still willing to trade some speed for a more durable execution if the proceeds and stability make the trade worth it.

Then there is the blended-capital version of the story. Northmarq announced on July 31 that it arranged $52.15 million of debt and equity capital for the 300-unit Maple Knoll Apartments in Westfield, Indiana. Even with the usual caution that comes with a deal announcement, the read-through is strong. More sponsors are getting transactions closed with mixed stacks rather than one clean senior loan. That does not mean the market is broken. It means the market is open, but only for borrowers willing to match the capital stack to today’s reality instead of yesterday’s assumptions.

Put those three deals together and the lender tone is fairly clear. Banks are in the market, but still disciplined and mostly focused on cleaner stories, stronger sponsors and relationships they already know. Life companies remain competitive for lower-leverage, high-quality multifamily and industrial, but the back end of the Treasury curve keeps them careful on proceeds and asset selection. CMBS remains available where scale, sponsorship and securitization logic all line up, but it is not acting like blind liquidity. Debt funds are still doing the heaviest lifting on construction completion, transitional business plans, recapitalizations and anything else that needs flexibility, timing or creativity.

The securitized market still deserves close attention, especially in multifamily. KBRA reported on July 31 that the overall delinquency rate in its rated private-label U.S. CMBS universe rose 29 basis points to 7.8 percent in July, while the distress rate climbed to 10.1 percent. More specifically for apartments, KBRA said the multifamily distress rate jumped 73 basis points in July after two months of declines, with twenty-three loans newly becoming distressed during the month. That is an important reminder that even inside the strongest property narrative in commercial real estate, old floating-rate loans, maturity pressure and underwriting that assumed faster NOI growth are still working through the system.

That is why it is too simplistic to say multifamily is either fine or broken. The better way to say it is that multifamily remains the preferred institutional story in commercial real estate, but it still contains plenty of loans that were capitalized for a friendlier rate regime. Properties with strong occupancy, credible sponsorship and realistic leverage can still attract capital. Properties that need a lot of forgiveness from the lender base are still being sorted into the debt-fund, structured-capital or workout buckets.

The Mortgage Bankers Association adds a second signal that helps frame the tone. MBA said on July 30 that second-quarter delinquency rates decreased across several major lender categories, including banks, life companies and CMBS. That is constructive because it says the system is still absorbing stress rather than compounding it. But it should not be read as a green light for loose credit. Falling delinquency rates do not automatically produce wider leverage, tighter spreads or easier committees. They mostly create a little more confidence that lenders can stay active without pretending risk has disappeared.

On the agency side, the most useful current update is less about a splashy property-level headline and more about pipeline evidence. Freddie Mac said in second-quarter results released July 30 that multifamily new business activity reached $18 billion in the quarter, up 58 percent from a year earlier, and that 66 percent of year-to-date activity was mission-driven affordable housing. Fannie Mae’s multifamily results, released July 29, showed a guaranty book of business of $544.6 billion, acquisition volume of $14.2 billion in the second quarter and a serious delinquency rate that improved to 0.60 percent from 0.78 percent in the prior quarter. That combination matters because it says the agencies are still a major source of steady permanent liquidity even when they are not producing the loudest daily headlines.

HUD and FHA also remain part of the live map, and not just as a policy footnote. Dwight’s Passaic refinancing is proof that the FHA-insured lane is still solving real executions. And the latest HUD FHA commercial mortgage portfolio data available show the multifamily insured book still enormous, with $140.4 billion of insurance in force as of May and only two new 60-plus-day multifamily defaults added that month. That does not mean FHA risk is trivial. It means the government-backed side of the apartment market is still operating from a very different credit posture than stressed private-label multifamily paper.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest official Treasury curve available at run time is 4.28 percent on the 2-year, 4.45 percent on the 5-year, 4.75 percent on the 10-year and 5.27 percent on the 30-year, with SOFR at 3.65 percent on the latest published print. Mortgage rates are still elevated, with Freddie Mac’s 30-year fixed average at 6.66 percent as of July 30. Fresh multifamily financing is still clearing through debt funds, HUD-backed refinancing and blended debt-plus-equity structures. CMBS remains open, but July performance data still point to stress, especially in multifamily. Agencies remain active and important, but selective private capital is still doing much of the visible work on harder deals.

One thing to watch this week is whether the long end of the Treasury curve can back off from these levels after the market has a full week to process the slower GDP print, sticky inflation and the next round of risk headlines. If the 10-year stays near 4.75 and the 30-year holds around 5.25 or higher, fixed-rate borrowers will probably keep hesitating and transitional lenders should keep winning share. If the long end eases even modestly, more permanent-debt borrowers may decide the market is not good, but good enough.

The Sunday takeaway is that the market is still functioning, but conviction matters. Nationally, the country is managing wildfire risk, public-safety shock and renewed pressure on household costs. In Debt Desk, the curve is still charging for duration, multifamily is still attracting capital but not uniformly, CMBS stress is still real, and the agencies continue to provide ballast. Capital is there. It is just asking harder questions before it shows up.
